title: The Psychology of Gollum: A Two-Agent Bargaining Model of the Self
text: The clinical literature treats Gollum as a cautionary tale about addiction. This is correct but incomplete. What the record actually documents — in unusual detail, thanks to two attentive hobbit observers — is a bargaining game between two selves sharing one body, and it rewards formal treatment.

title: The Psychology of Gollum: A Two-Agent Bargaining Model of the Self
text:
1 The setup
Model the individual as two agents. Sméagol has conventional preferences: food, memory of sunlight, the approval of others. Gollum has a single dominant preference with an infinite reservation price. The two alternate control of the body — the observable “arguments” are, in this reading, negotiation rounds over the allocation of future control.
The Ring functions as an asymmetric commitment device: every period it strengthens Gollum’s bargaining position and erodes Sméagol’s outside option. After five hundred years, Sméagol’s threat point is approximately zero. That he negotiates anything at all is remarkable.

title: The Psychology of Gollum: A Two-Agent Bargaining Model of the Self
text:
2 The Frodo intervention
The most interesting event in the dataset is exogenous: Frodo extends trust, addresses Sméagol by name, and — critically — creates external value for the Sméagol identity. For a period, the equilibrium visibly shifts: service is rendered, promises are kept, the Gollum agent is suppressed in daylight hours.
The mechanism matters for policy. Frodo did not strengthen Sméagol’s willpower (an intra-personal resource); he changed the payoff structure by making cooperation externally rewarded. Recovery, in this model, is not a triumph of will but a renegotiation under improved outside options.

title: The Psychology of Gollum: A Two-Agent Bargaining Model of the Self
section: 3 The relapse, and the stairs of Cirith Ungol
text:
3 The relapse, and the stairs of Cirith Ungol
The equilibrium collapses on contact with a third party who assigns the Sméagol identity zero value. One act of misrecognition — Sam’s accusation over the innocent matter of the rabbits — reprices Sméagol’s cooperative strategy to worthless, and Gollum resumes control permanently. Practitioners will recognise the pattern: the relapse is triggered not by the addictive good but by the withdrawal of the identity that made abstention worthwhile.

title: The Psychology of Gollum: A Two-Agent Bargaining Model of the Self
text:
4 Implication
If the self is a coalition, treatment is coalition management. Punishing the whole individual strengthens precisely the agent you wish to weaken — a result this author has verified, at length, in committee.

title: Dragon Hoards as Monetary Policy: Smaug and the Deflationary Trap
text: The standard histories treat the sack of Erebor as a security event. This is an accounting error. What Smaug executed in T.A. 2770 was the largest monetary contraction in recorded history: the withdrawal of an entire region’s specie stock from circulation, consolidated under a single balance sheet, held at zero velocity for 171 years (Reconstruction Economics 3018).

title: Dragon Hoards as Monetary Policy: Smaug and the Deflationary Trap
section: 1 The mechanics of a dragon-induced deflation
text:
1 The mechanics of a dragon-induced deflation
Dale and Erebor ran a metallic standard. When the gold left circulation — all of it, in one afternoon — the price level had nowhere to go but down, and the regional economy contracted along exactly the path the older literature on specie drains would predict (Grubb and Burrowes 2941). Wages fell, then employment, then the towns themselves. Lake-town’s subsequent two centuries of stagnation are usually blamed on geography. Geography did not eat the money supply.
What makes the case theoretically clean is the dragon’s demand function. Smaug held gold for neither transaction nor investment purposes; the hoard generated no lending, no seigniorage, nothing. His famous remark about knowing every coin in the pile (Baggins 2941) describes, in effect, a central banker running a full-reserve policy with a personal grudge. The literature on liquidity traps assumes the zero lower bound is a floor made of arithmetic; in Erebor it was a floor made of dragon.

title: Dragon Hoards as Monetary Policy: Smaug and the Deflationary Trap
text:
2 The reflation of 2941
The Battle of the Five Armies is conventionally studied as a military engagement. Monetarily, it was a disorderly quantitative easing: the entire consolidated hoard re-entered circulation within a decade, distributed across dwarven reconstruction, Dale’s rebuilding, and a modest fourteenth share carried west in two small chests (Baggins 2942). The regional recovery that followed was rapid, broad, and — as Gamgee (3020) notes in his study of post-war agricultural prices — mildly inflationary for exactly the reasons one would hope.
The episode thus provides both halves of the experiment: contraction by hoard, reflation by burglary. Few monetary interventions have been so thoroughly documented by their own instrument.

title: Dragon Hoards as Monetary Policy: Smaug and the Deflationary Trap
text:
3 What the auditor saw
This author’s field observation of the hoard remains, so far as he knows, the only physical inspection of a dragon-held reserve portfolio (Baggins 2941). Two findings deserve emphasis. First, mark-to-market valuation of a hoard is meaningless when the market comprises one dragon and no bids. Second — and practitioners underestimate this — the custody arrangements were impeccable. Nothing was missing. It is the velocity, not the security, of a nation’s money that keeps it alive.
There is a lesson here for modern reserve managers, but this author is a respectable hobbit and will let the reader draw it.

title: Dragon Hoards as Monetary Policy: Smaug and the Deflationary Trap
text:

title: Supply Chains of Middle-earth: Lembas, Logistics, and the Last Homely Warehouse
text: Every economy in Middle-earth solved provisioning differently: the Shire solved it with surplus and cellars, Rohan with mobility, Gondor with fortified granaries, and the Elves with a technology so far ahead of everyone else’s that it should have restructured the continent’s logistics — and didn’t.

title: Supply Chains of Middle-earth: Lembas, Logistics, and the Last Homely Warehouse
text:
1 The lembas anomaly
Lembas is, on the numbers, absurd. One cake sustains a working adult for a day; it keeps for months wrapped in a leaf; it weighs almost nothing. In supply-chain terms, elvish waybread collapses the tooth-to-tail ratio of any expedition to nearly zero. An army provisioned on lembas needs no baggage train, which means no roads, which means no predictable routes to ambush. It is a strategic technology.
Yet output never scaled. The chart below assembles the (entirely invented) production series this correspondent compiled from regional records. Hover over it: you’ll get crosshairs, exact values for every region at that date, and you can zoom into any period. Click a region in the legend to hide it.


Show the code behind this chart
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px

years = list(range(3001, 3022))
data = []
for region, base, trend, shock_year, shock in [
    ("Lothlórien",  84, 0.5, 3018, -30),
    ("Rivendell",   41, 0.3, 3018, -12),
    ("Mirkwood",    23, -0.8, 3010, -6),
    ("Grey Havens", 12, 0.9, None, 0),
]:
    level = base
    for y in years:
        level += trend
        if shock_year and y >= shock_year:
            level += shock / 3
        data.append({"year": y, "region": region,
                     "output": round(max(level, 1), 1)})

df = pd.DataFrame(data)

fig = px.line(
    df, x="year", y="output", color="region",
    labels={"year": "Third Age year", "output": "Output ('000 cakes)",
            "region": "Region"},
    color_discrete_sequence=["#2e5d43", "#8a6d3b", "#5b6b62", "#a63d40"],
)
fig.update_xaxes(showspikes=True, spikemode="across", spikedash="dot",
                 spikethickness=1)
fig.update_yaxes(showspikes=True, spikemode="across", spikedash="dot",
                 spikethickness=1, gridcolor="#e4e0d5")
fig.update_layout(
    hovermode="x unified",
    plot_bgcolor="white",
    font=dict(family="Source Sans 3, sans-serif"),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02),
    margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=30, b=10),
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 1: Waybread output by region, Third Age 3001–3021 (thousand cakes/year). Entirely fictional data; hover for values.




Note the structural break at 3018: the War disrupted Lothlórien’s output — and the industry never recovered its peak, because the workforce emigrated. Which brings us to the real constraint.

title: Supply Chains of Middle-earth: Lembas, Logistics, and the Last Homely Warehouse
text:
2 Why the technology never diffused
Three hypotheses circulate in the literature, of unequal quality:

Recipe secrecy (weak). Trade secrets leak over ten thousand years. Something else binds.
Non-transferable inputs (stronger). If production requires inputs that exist only where Elves and their particular ecology persist — a terroir theory of waybread — then the technology is land-linked and cannot be licensed out.
The gift-good hypothesis (strongest). Lembas was never a commodity. It moves only as a gift, between parties in specific relationships. The Elves were not running an industry below capacity; they were refusing, on principle, to have an industry at all. As with the Eagles, the constraint is institutional, not technical.

title: Supply Chains of Middle-earth: Lembas, Logistics, and the Last Homely Warehouse
text:
3 The practitioner’s postscript
For actual expedition provisioning, this correspondent’s advice is unchanged: take the lembas gratefully, count on nothing you cannot grow or carry, and remember that the finest logistics innovation of the Third Age remains the humble coney, stewed, with taters. PO-TA-TOES.

title: About
text:
This is a mock site — a full-featured rehearsal for the migration of The Leap Journal from Blogger to Quarto. Everything here exercises a real planned feature: listings, announcements, author pages, comments, copyable citations, PDF downloads, search, topic filters, and executable charts.
The content is deliberately fictional. The Leap Journal does not, to our knowledge, employ any wizards.

title: About
text:
What to poke at

Search (magnifying glass in the navbar) — full text of every article.
Topic filters on the Articles page — click a category, or type in the filter box.
Authors — tiles for each contributor, each with their own page.
On any article: the Download PDF button, the Cite this article block (copy the BibTeX with one click), and the comment section at the bottom.
The supply chains article has an interactive chart — hover over it.
The dragon hoards article has real inline citations and a bibliography.

title: About
section: How to publish on this site
text:
How to publish on this site
Publishing here is: write a text file, push it to GitHub. There is no CMS, no dashboard, no server. This section is the whole workflow.

One-time setup
git clone git@github.com:cynicalcyanide/leapblog-mock.git
cd leapblog-mock
python3.13 -m venv .venv && ./.venv/bin/pip install jupyter plotly pandas
You need Quarto installed. The Python step is only needed if your article runs code (charts); prose-only authors can skip it.


Writing an article
Every article is one folder under posts/, holding one file called index.qmd plus any images:
posts/
  my-new-article/
    index.qmd
    figure-1.png
An index.qmd is ordinary Markdown with a small metadata header:
---
title: "My New Article"
description: "One sentence shown in listings and search results."
author:
  - name: Samwise Gamgee
    url: ../../authors/samwise.html
date: 2026-09-10
categories: [economics, supply chains]
image: figure-1.png
---

Write normally. **Bold**, *italics*, [links](https://example.com),
## headings, > quotes — it's just Markdown.
That header is the single source of truth: it feeds the listings, the topic filters, the author page, search, the citation block, and the PDF — you never configure those per-article.


Images
Drop image files into your article’s folder and reference them by filename:
![Lembas output collapsed after 3018.](figure-1.png)
The text in brackets becomes the caption. Images travel with the article’s folder, so nothing ever breaks when things move.


Graphs
Two options:

Static image — make the chart anywhere, export a PNG, include it like any image (above).
Executable chart — put the actual Python/R code in the article. The code runs when the site builds; readers get an interactive figure (hover values, zoom). See the supply chains article and click “Show the code” for a complete working example to copy. If you do this, run the article once locally before pushing (see Previewing, below) so the result is cached for the build.



The PDF
You do nothing. Every article is automatically typeset into a downloadable PDF at build time — the Download PDF button appears on its own. The same goes for the citation block, the comment section, search indexing, and the listings.


Citations (optional)
To cite formally, add a references.bib file to your article folder, declare it in the header (bibliography: references.bib), and cite in the text with @key. The bibliography formats itself at the end of the article. The dragon hoards article is a working example.


Previewing
From the repository folder:
QUARTO_PYTHON=.venv/bin/python quarto preview
Your browser opens a live version of the site; it refreshes as you save. (Prose-only articles can drop the QUARTO_PYTHON= prefix.)


Publishing
git add posts/my-new-article
git commit -m "New article: My New Article"
git push
That’s it. GitHub rebuilds the site automatically and your article is live — listings, PDF, citation block and all — in about two minutes. No one needs to press anything else.

title: Shieldmaidens and the Rohirrim Labour Market
text: Rohan’s principal export is cavalry. Its principal labour-market institution is a hard occupational bar excluding half the adult population from the cavalry. This column examines how that worked out.

title: Shieldmaidens and the Rohirrim Labour Market
text:
1 The steady-state cost
The static loss is the familiar one: talent misallocation. The kingdom’s defence output was produced from an artificially restricted labour pool, with predictable effects on quality at the margin. The shadow price of the restriction was invisible in peacetime — restrictions usually are — because the counterfactual soldier is a statistic and the norm is a tradition with songs.

title: Shieldmaidens and the Rohirrim Labour Market
text:
2 The stress test
The Pelennor Fields provided the out-of-sample test. Two observations:

The binding constraint bit at the extreme tail. The single most consequential combat action of the battle — the destruction of the Witch-king — was performed by an excluded worker, operating outside the licensing regime, who had entered the sector through what economists call irregular channels and what Rohan calls disguise.
The prophecy was a market signal everyone misread. “Not by the hand of man shall he fall” was, in retrospect, a standing arbitrage opportunity: an adversary invulnerable only to the excluded category. A rational personnel office would have recruited against it. Tradition priced it at zero.

title: Shieldmaidens and the Rohirrim Labour Market
text:
3 The general point
Occupational restrictions are usually defended on average-quality grounds and usually costed in average terms. But defence — like several other sectors — is a tail-risk business. The value of an open labour market is not the mean worker it adds; it is the specific worker you cannot predict needing. You do not know, in advance, whose hand the job requires.
Rohan has since reformed its recruitment practices. The songs, it must be said, adapted immediately; the pension system is taking longer.

title: The Ecology of Middle-earth: Old-growth Governance from Fangorn to Mirkwood
text: Middle-earth offers ecologists something modern datasets rarely do: forests with continuous institutional records running to tens of thousands of years, and stakeholders old enough to remember every policy intervention personally. The comparison between Fangorn and Mirkwood is, in effect, a natural experiment in woodland governance.

title: The Ecology of Middle-earth: Old-growth Governance from Fangorn to Mirkwood
text:
1 Fangorn: common-pool resources with shepherds
Fangorn is the canonical case of a common-pool resource managed by resident stewards with effectively infinite time horizons. The Ents do not discount the future in any measurable way; when your deliberative assembly takes a month to agree on the agenda, quarterly thinking is not a risk.
Three institutional features stand out:

Monitoring is continuous and ambulatory. The shepherds walk the resource. Enforcement is personal, proportionate, and occasionally involves throwing rocks at industrial facilities.
Membership is closed but succession is a crisis. The absence of Entwives is, in economic terms, a catastrophic failure of demographic replacement that no governance structure can indefinitely survive. Institutions require heirs.
Exit from passivity is discontinuous. Fangorn tolerated marginal encroachment for centuries, then internalised an entire externality in one afternoon by demolishing Isengard. Regulators everywhere should note the shape of that response function: flat, flat, flat, vertical.

title: The Ecology of Middle-earth: Old-growth Governance from Fangorn to Mirkwood
section: 2 Mirkwood: what happens under absentee pressure
text:
2 Mirkwood: what happens under absentee pressure
Greenwood the Great became Mirkwood not through harvesting but through a hostile change in effective ownership. A single unaccountable actor established residence at Dol Guldur, and the ecosystem repriced immediately: species composition shifted toward spiders of unusual size, path networks decayed, and the river acquired properties best described as non-standard.
The elven response — retreat northward, fortify, tax passing traffic — is recognisably the strategy of a minority stakeholder who cannot dislodge the majority polluter and settles for enclave quality. It works, for the enclave. The rest of the forest carries the cost.

title: The Ecology of Middle-earth: Old-growth Governance from Fangorn to Mirkwood
text:
3 What travels
Strip the wizards out and the lesson is portable: forest outcomes track the time horizon of whoever holds effective control. Patient residents with enforcement power produce old growth. Absentee extraction produces spiders. The policy instrument that matters is not the harvesting quota but the identity, tenure, and patience of the controlling party.
Further fieldwork is planned, pending the availability of the author, who is expected back around the turn of the age.

title: Eagles as Critical Transport Infrastructure: Why We Can’t Just Fly Everywhere
text: No question is put to this author more often, at conferences and in taverns, than the Eagle Question: why didn’t you simply fly? The question is understandable and the answer is institutional, so naturally nobody stays for it. Here it is in writing.

title: Eagles as Critical Transport Infrastructure: Why We Can’t Just Fly Everywhere
text:
1 Infrastructure with sovereignty
The Great Eagles present as transport capacity: heavy-lift, all-weather, unmatched speed over hostile terrain. The error is to model them as infrastructure, when they are in fact a sovereign provider — a self-governing polity that occasionally, at its own discretion, performs airlift.
The distinction is everything. Infrastructure has a schedule and a price. A sovereign provider has interests, risk tolerances, and the right of refusal. There is no contract, no tariff, no service-level agreement — every Eagle intervention on record is a gift, and gift economies do not scale into logistics networks.

title: Eagles as Critical Transport Infrastructure: Why We Can’t Just Fly Everywhere
text:
2 The airspace problem
Even granting goodwill, the corridor analysis is grim. A direct flight to the objective traverses continuously surveilled airspace defended by interceptors specifically bred for the role. Strategic transport that must survive contested airspace is not transport; it is an air campaign, with an air campaign’s probability of success and an air campaign’s tendency to announce itself.
The historical uses of Eagle capacity — extraction of stranded persons from towers, pinnacles, and volcanoes — share a profile: short duration, low predictability, terminal urgency. This is search-and-rescue, and search-and-rescue is precisely the mission gift-economy capacity is good for.

title: Eagles as Critical Transport Infrastructure: Why We Can’t Just Fly Everywhere
text:
3 The policy failure worth naming
The real lesson is that Middle-earth’s Free Peoples never built the boring alternative: roads. Reliable, dull, contract-governed surface logistics would have changed more outcomes than any eagle. Civilisations are tempted to solve infrastructure gaps with heroic capacity — the sovereign provider that shows up at the last moment — because heroes are cheaper than maintenance budgets, right up until they decline the mission.
Build the roads. Thank the Eagles. Do not confuse the two.
